newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Cyclone shuts 200,000-bpd Australian crude output.
newsitem.headline: Cyclone shuts 200,000-bpd Australian crude output.

text.p: The loss of more than 200,000 barrels per day in Australian oil producton is underpinning sentiment in the Asian light sweet crude market, but price reaction has been muted, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Traders said they expected only limited price reaction until the next trading month picks up some time in the next 10 days.
For the time being, reaction was muted as most refineries were still working out preferable crude grades for delivery in February and March.
"There is no reason to buy now because we are between trading months," said one trader at a major. "People are just waking up."

Indonesian grades were unlikely to start trading until next week, after term nominations were made. Middle East crudes were just starting talk for March and light sweet grades were not really trading either, market sources said.
Operator Broken Hill Pty Ltd confirmed on Tuesday it had stopped production from the offshore 70,000 barrels per day (bpd) Griffin oil field to avoid the path of Cyclone Rachel.
Operator Woodside Petroleum Ltd also confirmed it had disconnected the floating production unit at the 90,000 bpd Cossack field.
The West Australian Petroleum Pty Ltd (WAPET) said on Monday it was planning to shut down both the 10-15,000 bpd Barrow Island and the 30,000 bpd Thevenard fields.
Traders said the 10,000 bpd Wanoo field was also shut down.
The closures were the second in two weeks for most of the fields after their floating platforms were disconnected last week to avoid Cyclone Phil.

Traders said some ships loading crude had also been affected by the latest closures, but schedules were not too cramped yet. Rachel marks the fourth cyclone of the 1996/97 season, which runs from November to March.
The latest cyclone is packing winds of 180 kph and is moving southwest at 15 kph towards Port Hedland on the western coast.
Traders said the shut down news was clearly underpinning sentiment for light sweet grades and their benchmark Tapis crude oil, which is already valued at a fresh five-year high.
The Malaysian crude was assessed Tuesday at $27.20/$27.40 per barrel, surpassing the previous highs hit late last year.
The crude last traded for February at a market premium of $1.60 per barrel, one of the highest premiums in more than a year, some traders said.

Most of the support is coming from product demand for middle distillates, prompting refiners to run at maximum output levels. Tapis and the Australian grades are rich in middle distillate yields, although some of the Australian grades are more geared to naphtha.
Refining margins were strong, largely supported by products demand, which would underpin the market, the traders said.
In addition, China has been a very strong buyer of a range of Asian crudes in the past six weeks and was the end buyer of the latest Tapis deal at $1.60.
"Their inventories are relatively low because they were hoping that the absolute price would come down. But it didn't happen," a trader said.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
